title: The Homecoming Tick Check: A Two-Person Routine for Clothes, Skin, and Pets
subtitle: Daily Read | A calm, repeatable handoff can make post-outdoor checks easier—without turning them into a source of alarm.
imageAlt: Two friends at a home entryway check a jacket and a dog after returning from a walk; a mirror and laundry basket are nearby.
imageConcept: A warm, lived-in entryway in late afternoon: two friends have just come back from a wooded walk, one checking a dog’s coat while the other puts outdoor clothes beside a laundry basket. A wall mirror and soft natural light make the scene practical, relaxed and unhurried.
body: Make the return home part of the plan

A tick check is easiest to remember when it has a place in the day. Rather than trying to inspect everything outdoors or turning the first moments at home into a medical drill, use the transition back indoors: outdoor clothes and gear get set aside, people check their own skin, and pets get a look-over. Think of it as a handoff between the outing and the rest of the day.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends checking your body, clothing, gear and pets after coming indoors. It also says showering within two hours may help reduce the risk of Lyme disease and offers a convenient opportunity to check for ticks.[1] That is a useful window, not a deadline or a guarantee. If a shower is not practical, a careful check still makes sense. Tick bites do not all lead to illness, and a routine should help people notice a possible bite—not make every outdoor outing feel dangerous.
First stop: clothes, shoes and gear

Choose a spot near the entrance where outdoor items can be handled without being mixed into clean laundry. Check the visible surfaces and seams of pants, socks, shirts and jackets; take a look at shoes, bags and other gear that came along. Ticks can travel indoors on clothing or equipment, so this step matters even if nobody noticed a bite outside.[1]

If the clothes are dry, the CDC advises putting them in a dryer on high heat for 10 minutes to kill ticks. Damp clothes may need additional time.[1] Follow the garment’s care instructions, and don’t assume a short tumble is enough for wet items. If you cannot dry them immediately, keep the outdoor clothes apart from clean ones until you can deal with them. The point is a clear sequence, not a perfect laundry system: set items aside, inspect what you can, then use the recommended drying step when appropriate.

A small basket or a designated hook can make this routine easier to repeat. Keep it practical for the household: the best place is one people will actually use.
A personal check, with privacy intact

Each person can check their own skin in good light, using hands and eyes to look and feel over the body. Pay attention to places that are easy to miss, including the scalp and hairline, in and around the ears, under the arms, around the waist, inside the belly button, behind the knees, and between the legs. A full-length mirror and a hand mirror can help with areas that are hard to see. The CDC recommends a full-body check after coming indoors.[1]

A second person can offer to hold a mirror or help with a hard-to-see area—but only if that help is welcome. Ask first, be specific about the offer, and accept “no” without making it awkward. A partner, family member or friend does not need to inspect someone else’s body to make the routine useful. People can adapt the check to their mobility, vision, comfort and privacy needs: a seated check, a handheld mirror, or a trusted helper can all be options.

Showering soon after returning can be a convenient moment to check. It may also wash off unattached ticks, but it is not a replacement for looking carefully over the skin.[1]

Dogs and other pets can bring ticks inside, so include them in the homecoming sequence. Run your hands through the coat while looking and feeling for anything unusual, taking care around areas where ticks may be harder to spot, such as ears, the collar area, under the legs and between toes. The CDC specifically includes pets in its after-outdoors check guidance.[1]

Keep the check calm and suited to the animal. A pet that dislikes prolonged handling may do better with a few brief passes, treats or a familiar grooming routine. If you find an attached tick, use removal guidance appropriate for that animal, or contact a veterinarian if you are unsure how to proceed. Don’t use a product on a pet unless it is intended for that animal and you have followed its label or veterinary advice. The aim is to notice and respond—not to make the check stressful for either of you.
If you find an attached tick

Remove an attached tick as soon as possible. CDC guidance is to use fine-tipped tweezers, grasp the tick close to the skin, and pull upward with steady, even pressure. Avoid twisting or jerking. The CDC advises against trying to make a tick detach with heat, petroleum jelly or nail polish.[2] If mouthparts remain and cannot be removed easily, avoid digging into the skin; seek advice from a healthcare professional if you are concerned.

After removal, clean the bite area and your hands. If useful, note the date and where the exposure happened, or take a photo of the tick. These details may help if you later contact a clinician. A tick bite is not by itself proof that a person has an infection, and the next step depends on the circumstances and local risks. If you are uncertain what to do, a healthcare professional can advise you.
Know what to watch for—and when to call

In the weeks after a bite or a relevant outdoor exposure, pay attention to how you feel. Lyme disease symptoms can include fever, chills, headache, fatigue, muscle and joint aches, and swollen lymph nodes; a rash may or may not be present.[3] The CDC advises seeking medical attention if symptoms develop after a recent tick bite or possible exposure.[3] A rash is not the only reason to ask for care, and the absence of a rash should not be used to dismiss other concerning symptoms.

This is a reason to be observant, not to diagnose yourself from a checklist. Write down when the bite or outing happened and what symptoms you notice, then share that information with a healthcare professional. If someone feels seriously unwell, seek urgent medical help. For general questions about an attached tick, removal or possible symptoms, contact a clinician rather than relying on a household routine to settle a medical concern.
Make the doorway do the remembering

At the next return from a trail, garden or other place where ticks may be present, try the sequence once with whoever shares the home: outdoor clothes and gear in one spot, a personal check with good light or a mirror, then a pet check if there is an animal in the household. Ask before offering hands-on help, and let each person choose what feels comfortable. If you find a tick, use the removal steps and decide whether medical advice is needed. Afterward, notice which part of the setup made the routine easier—and adjust that one thing. A basket, a better-lit mirror or a reminder near the entry may be enough. The goal is a usable habit, not a perfect inspection.
